question.:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}$ at the point where $x=2$ is{{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-{x}^{2}+10x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10-2x.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (10-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2(x-5)}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}} \\  & =-\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(-\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}})|}_{x=2} \\  & =\frac{10-2(2)}{2\sqrt{-(2{)}^{2}+10(2)}} \\  & =\frac{6}{2\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
